I need to write a JUnit 4 test class called ToStringStyleTest covering the ToStringStyle abstract class, testing it through its public static constants and by creating a test subclass to access protected methods.

Since ToStringStyle has many protected methods, I'll create an inner `ToStringStyleImpl` subclass in the same package so I can test the append overloads, appendSuper, appendToString, appendStart, appendEnd, and the protected getters/setters directly.

I also need boundary tests for removeLastFieldSeparator and null-to-empty-string conversions across the various setter methods like setArrayStart, setArrayEnd, setArraySeparator, setContentStart, setContentEnd, and setFieldNameValueSeparator.

I should also verify basic properties of the predefined static style singletons (DEFAULT_STYLE, MULTI_LINE_STYLE, NO_FIELD_NAMES_STYLE, SHORT_PREFIX_STYLE, SIMPLE_STYLE), since their protected getters are accessible from the same package. I'll write comprehensive tests targeting branch coverage without needing mocking libraries, since these can be exercised directly.

I'm laying out the test methods systematically by functionality, tracing through edge cases like how appendToString behaves when the content markers aren't found in the string, since indexOf/lastIndexOf returning -1 changes which branch gets hit.

I also need a test case where fieldSeparatorAtStart is enabled, requiring a buffer pre-filled with a separator to exercise the removeLastFieldSeparator path, plus a test for appendStart with a null object.

Then I'll cover appendEnd scenarios for both separator-removal and no-removal cases, followed by direct tests of removeLastFieldSeparator covering matches, non-matches, short buffers, and zero-length separators. Finally I'll test appendObject for both null and non-null values.

I'm continuing to list out remaining test cases: primitive type appends (byte, char, double, float, boolean), class name appending variations, identity hash code appending, and full detail flag checks.

Now I'm thinking about the registry tests — since getRegistry(), isRegistered(), register(), and unregister() are package-private static methods, I can call them directly from the test class without reflection. I'll verify registering an object marks it as registered and unregistering clears it, plus check that null handling doesn't throw since WeakHashMap permits null keys.

One concern is that REGISTRY is a ThreadLocal, so state could leak across tests running in the same thread — I should unregister test objects after each test to keep things isolated. For cyclic detection, I plan to manually register a value, call appendInternal, and confirm the cyclic-object path is triggered instead of appendDetail for non-primitive types.

Since appendInternal is protected and the test class lives in the same package, I can call it directly on any ToStringStyle instance without needing a subclass — protected access in Java includes package-level visibility.

This means I don't need the ToStringStyleImpl subclass at all. I can just use the public DEFAULT_STYLE singleton (a ToStringStyle reference) and invoke protected methods on it directly, though mutating its state for the test is a bit risky since it's shared elsewhere.

Tracing through the array detail logic for the null-element test case: the loop appends "<null>" for the null entry, then a separator, then the plain string "b" via appendInternal, yielding "{<null>,b}" wrapped by the array start/end markers.

Checking the full-detail array test now, confirming that when fullDetail is true the branch correctly routes through appendDetail for the array.

Tracing through appendDetail for the Object[] branch confirms it produces "{x,y}" which combines to "field={x,y}," matching expectations, and String[] arrays are indeed valid instances of Object[] in Java so the cast works correctly.

Checking appendSummary against the expected "<String>" output confirms it matches by combining the start/end markers with the short class name. I'm now verifying the primitive int array reflection test, which uses Array.getLength and Array.get to iterate and box each int into an Integer before appending.

Since item isn't registered yet, it gets temporarily registered, falls to the else-branch since it's not a collection/map/array, appends the value directly, then unregisters it afterward - producing "1" then "2" then "3", matching the expected "{1,2,3}" output with the configured separators and brackets.

For the cyclic object test, since the object is manually registered beforehand and isn't a Number/Boolean/Character, the cyclic-detection branch triggers instead, calling appendCyclicObject which delegates to ObjectUtils.identityToString - producing something like "java.lang.Object@<hash>" without touching the register/unregister lifecycle itself.

Since appendInternal returns early in this branch, it never calls unregister either, so the object stays registered until my test manually unregisters it in the finally block - which matches what I wrote. Now I need to check the equivalent test for Number/Boolean/Character-typed values that are pre-registered.

Boolean and Character cases follow the same logic, matching expected outputs "true" and "x".

Now checking the overload resolution for appendSummary(Object) - passing a String literal resolves unambiguously to the Object overload rather than Object[] since there's no array match.

Now I'm looking at the appendToString_WithContent test expecting "Foo[bar=1]".

Then appendFieldSeparator appends "," giving "bar=1,", matching expectations. For the fieldSeparatorAtStart test, I'm tracing how it strips the trailing separator from "existing," before appending the new data, then re-adds the separator afterward.

Checking appendStart with fieldSeparatorAtStart true: it appends the class name, identity hashcode, content-start bracket, then the leading separator, so the result should end with "[,", which I'll verify with an endsWith check rather than exact match given hashcode variability.

Now verifying appendEnd: with default settings the trailing field separator gets stripped before the closing bracket is appended, giving "field=1]"; with fieldSeparatorAtEnd true, no stripping occurs so it becomes "field=1,]" instead. Then I move to checking the removeLastFieldSeparator behavior when the separator is null.

Setting the separator to null effectively makes its length zero, so the buffer remains untouched regardless of content since the zero-length check short-circuits the operation. Similarly, when the separator is longer than the buffer itself, or when the buffer is empty, the method skips removal entirely and leaves the buffer as-is—all consistent with expected test outcomes. Now I'm checking the matching case where the buffer actually ends with the separator, confirming the removal logic triggers correctly there.

I verify Java's StringBuffer formatting for appended doubles and floats produces values like "1.0" without extra suffixes, matching expected test strings. Then I move to checking how a collection's toString() renders in the expected output format for a single-element list.

For the boolean parameter ambiguity, I confirm that casting list to Object before calling the append method avoids any overload resolution issues, even though it's likely unnecessary since lists aren't arrays.

Now I'm checking the full-detail-false case for a String value: the summary format produces "<String>" using the short class name wrapped in angle brackets, so the full buffer reads "field=<String>,". I'll tighten the assertion to check exact equality rather than just prefix/suffix matching for a stronger test.

I also want to verify the default field values match the source — useFieldNames, useClassName, useShortClassName, useIdentityHashCode, defaultFullDetail, arrayContentDetail, and the separator flags all need to align with their documented defaults.

Going through the specific style subclasses now: NoFieldNameToStringStyle only toggles useFieldNames off, ShortPrefixToStringStyle flips useShortClassName on and useIdentityHashCode off, and SimpleToStringStyle disables className/identityHashCode/fieldNames while blanking out the content start/end markers — each matching their respective test expectations.

For MultiLineToStringStyle, the content start, field separator, and content end use the platform line separator, but the test only verifies that field separator appears at the start, so it's safe regardless of platform.

I also need to double check the imports and annotations are complete, and make sure there's no ambiguity in the overloaded append call when passing a null object alongside a Boolean argument.

Checking the four-argument append overloads to confirm that a String value paired with a Boolean resolves uniquely to the Object version, since it's not an array type and the signature count differs from the primitive array overloads.

Checking the long[] and other typed array overloads resolve correctly, then confirming the null-cast tests for each array type (Object[], long[], int[], etc.) match my code's explicit casts to disambiguate overload resolution.

Now verifying each primitive-type append call (int, short, byte, char, double, float, boolean) matches its distinct overload exactly without boxing ambiguity, then moving on to test the appendFieldStart behavior with field names disabled.

I confirm with useFieldNames false or fieldName null, appendFieldStart skips the name and only appendDetail and the trailing field separator get written, matching the expected "5," result in both test cases, and note that appendFieldStart being protected isn't an issue since it's only invoked indirectly through public append methods.

Checking the rest of the protected method calls—removeLastFieldSeparator, reflectionAppendArrayDetail, appendInternal, appendSummary, appendClassName, appendIdentityHashCode, isFullDetail, getShortClassName, and the various setters/getters—all are fine to call directly since they're same-package access, as are the package-private static register/unregister/isRegistered methods on ToStringStyle.

I'm weighing whether an explicit import of ToStringStyle is needed even though the test class lives in the same package—technically redundant but legal in Java, similar to explicitly importing java.lang.String, so I could add it for clarity without causing a compile error.

Now I'm reviewing the full set of tests once more for annotation correctness, unique method names, and proper imports, and considering adding Thai comments where behavior depends on things like ObjectUtils.identityToString formatting.

Given the large number of tests (around 90), I'm deciding to group them by category rather than list each one individually when building the final summary table, since the instructions ask for a concise table showing which branches/conditions each test method covers.
